Hi Jenny,

At the moment dartR does not have the capability of working with the counts data. You will need to turn to  radiator (an R package for RADseq Data Exploration, Manipulation and Visualization) for this.

We have a policy of not writing scripts for dartR that delve into DArT processes below what is provided to users by DArT in their routine reports. Users can request the count data specifically, but this is not routine. I understand that DArT is considering providing the count data in their routine reporting (via OneDArT) so this might change. It would certainly be good for some applications such a detecting and filtering sex linked markers.

If you have DIY'ed some scripts for this, perhaps consider contributing them to dartR :)

Sorry we cannot be of more help at this time.

A

glRef <- gl.filter.locmetric(gl, lower=5, upper=100, metric="AvgCountRef")

cheers,
carlo

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabrielle,

One of the difficulties with filtering on call rate is that you may have 20% missing data based on the total number of loci as the denominator, then you take 10% of them out by filtering, and find that you don't have 10% left. This is because the denominator on the percentage estimate changes when you delete loci during filtering. If you want 10% left at the end of the filtering (as opposed to deleting 10% of what you start with), you need to reapply the filter repeatedly until the end value stabilizes.

I suspect that is what is going on anyway.

Arthur

Hi Everyone,

I realize that this is not a direct dartR question, but since dartR masters so many common genetic conversions in R, I was hoping to get some advice.

My question is, does dartR or any other program have a way of reading multiple fastas and converting to genind/genlight formats while properly converting the ambiguity codes?

It is easy to read genome-scale fastas in R using the apex functions read.multiFASTA() and then multidna2genind() to convert to a genind object. Unfortunately, this relies on DNAbin2genind and seems to take the ambiguity codes for say heterozygous states (e.g., w = A/T) and codes them as NA in the genind object. Of course that is unacceptable for any popgen studies.

If anyone has any suggestions for doing this for a folder of fasta loci, I would be really appreciative.

Thanks so much!

Frank

Hi Gabriella,

The table produced by gl.report.hwe() is a data.table object, see more information here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/data.table/vignettes/datatable-intro.html.

A data.table object is in almost all aspects the same as a data.frame object. One of the differences is that a data.table when printed, only the beginning and end of the object are displayed. To displayed the first 100 rows of the data.table you could use:
library(dartR)
test <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
res <- gl.report.hwe(test)
print(res,topn  = 100)

I think, this solves Q1 to Q4.

Your interpretation from Q5 is correct.

Cheers,
Luis

Luis

# subsetting loci that are significant in all populations
report_pop <- report_hwe[which(report_hwe$npop==nPop(test)),]
# getting unique loci names and counting them
length(unique(report_pop$Locus))
# [1] 17

# Filtering loci in HWE.

                     subset = "each",
                     n.pop.threshold = nPop(test))

Hi Anna,

Sorry for the late reply.

You can calculate the effective number of alleles using the dartR function gl.report.diversity(), as shown in the code below. This function is based on the paper of Bill Sherwin:
Sherwin, William B., et al. "Information theory broadens the spectrum of molecular ecology and evolution." Trends in ecology & evolution 32.12 (2017): 948-963.

The effective number of alleles is very sensitive to rare alleles and unequal sample sizes, so it can be biased if you don't have a large sample size. The best way to deal with this is calculating allelic richness using the rarefaction method as implemented in the package Hierfstat, as shown in the code below. If you want to know more about how allelic richness is calculated, see:
El Mousadik, A., and R. J. Petit. "High level of genetic differentiation for allelic richness among populations of the argan tree [Argania spinosa (L.) Skeels] endemic to Morocco." Theoretical and applied genetics 92.7 (1996): 832-839.

library(dartR)
test <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
res <- gl.report.diversity(test)
# this is the effective number of alleles
res_2 <- res$zero_D_alpha
# printing results
res_2

library(hierfstat)
test_2 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
# filtering loci with all missing data
test_2 <- gl.filter.allna(test_2)
#converting to genind
genind_2 <- gl2gi(test_2)
#converting to hierfstat
hierfstat <- genind2hierfstat(genind_2)
# calculating allelic richness

Hi Eliane,

Based on the data you  sent me, the problem was that confidence intervals using the JackKnife method only works in populations with more than two individuals.

I have fixed this bug, so when a population has less than three individuals JackKnife confidence intervals are NA.

To use this updated function, you should install the developing version of dartR by typing in the R console:

library(dartR)
gl.install.vanilla.dartR(flavour = "dev")

Cheers,
Luis
